summary: Autonomous driving is the visible front, but AI runs through freight matching, maritime navigation, transit operations, and aviation. Who tracks it: the safety regulators and standards bodies are the primary record, with the operators' own published data layered on top.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in transportation and warehousing (NAICS 48-49) at 13.0% of firms in the latest reading, up from 7.9% in the prior period. The survey asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and it has covered the sector since September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material, and it describes the sector as a whole rather than any single mode.

The most visible deployment is autonomous driving. Aurora describes the Aurora Driver as hardware and software backed by verifiable AI, integrated into fleets, and quotes a Werner executive on a pilot hauling freight between Fort Worth and El Paso under a hybrid model of professional drivers plus the driverless system. Waymo, which began as the Google Self-Driving Car Project in 2009 and served its first fully autonomous rides in 2015, publishes a safety program and frames autonomous driving as a way to reduce traffic fatalities, aligning its work with the U.S. Department of Transportation National Roadway Safety Strategy. The American Trucking Associations is the trade body tracking policy and adoption for autonomous freight and AI logistics, with more than 37,000 members.

AI is also deployed in the less visible layers of the sector. Samsara says its connected operations platform serves 20,000+ operations and reports 380,000+ accidents prevented through AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, and automated coaching, alongside predictive analytics and equipment management. C.H. Robinson describes autonomous logistics orchestration in which a supply chain analyzes, decides, executes, and improves continuously across every shipment, and runs an AI assistant on its site. Wärtsilä cites AI-driven predictive analytics among the tools it offers marine customers, and Airbus describes a decarbonised, connected and autonomous future for aerospace built on digitised operations.

Regulators are setting the terms. EASA's Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0 sets out its vision for safety and ethical considerations of AI in aviation, with an action plan, conceptual guidance deliverables, and anticipated rulemaking, and it is amended once a year. The International Maritime Organization adopted a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships in May 2026, effective 1 July 2026, a goal-based framework covering design, construction, operation, and certification to safety and environmental standards equivalent to conventional ships, with voluntary guidance intended to facilitate a future transition into a mandatory instrument. The IMO notes that at present there are no commercially operating, internationally trading SOLAS cargo ships that operate autonomously or remotely controlled, though trials have shown larger such ships are feasible.

On money and returns, the sources are thin. The clearest quantified outcome is Samsara's 380,000+ accidents prevented. Aurora's page quotes a customer calling early pilot results impressive and cites projected five fold growth in freight volumes between 2010 and 2050 as making autonomous transport a necessity. Wärtsilä notes it will supply 282 MW of onsite power for a U.S. data center as AI growth intensifies demand for reliable power, a reminder that the sector both deploys AI and supplies its infrastructure. No source here reports a sector-wide ROI figure, and none should be inferred.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few observations. Adoption as measured by the Census Bureau remains a minority of firms but is rising. The documented deployments cluster around autonomy, fleet safety and telematics, freight matching, predictive maintenance, and vessel and aircraft operations, which suggests the entry points are operational rather than experimental. The regulatory posture differs sharply by mode: aviation AI passes through EASA's roadmap and rulemaking, maritime autonomy now has the IMO's MASS Code, and trucking autonomy is tracked by the American Trucking Associations. The sources do not describe costs, failure rates, or labor effects, so those questions remain open on this record.

https://www.samsara.com/.brief: Samsara claims its connected operations platform supports more than 20,000 operations in improving safety, cutting costs, and running smarter. The platform analyzes data to provide AI-driven alerts, predictive analytics, and actionable insights that help spot risks and optimize operations. According to Samsara, its AI-powered dash cams, real-time in-cab alerts, automated coaching, and other safety technologies have prevented over 380,000 accidents. The system includes cameras and video AI, multicam support, driver experience tools, driver coaching, drowsiness detection, safety reporting & insights, and equipment management.

https://www.trucking.org/.brief: ATA, the American Trucking Association, says it is the largest and most comprehensive national trade association for trucking. It reports that Miguel Corral, a UPS driver, was named Bendix Grand Champion at the 2026 National Truck Driving & Step Van Championships. ATA says it has more than 37,000 members, including carriers, suppliers, shippers, and professionals, and that it works to influence government policy, educate stakeholders, and host events that bring together all parts of the industry.

https://www.wartsila.com/.brief: Wärtsilä claims it is a global leader in innovative technologies and lifecycle solutions for the marine and energy markets. The company says it already has most of the technology needed to decarbonise, from engines that can run flexibly on low- and zero-carbon fuels to AI-driven predictive analytics. Wärtsilä is using these tools to help customers take the next step on their decarbonisation journey.

https://www.easa.europa.eu/en/domains/re.brief: The EASA has published an Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0 that outlines the Agency's approach to safety and ethical considerations for AI in aviation. The roadmap provides an action plan for the EASA AI Programme, including conceptual guidance and anticipated rulemaking activities, and serves as a basis for stakeholder discussions. As a living document, it will be updated annually and refined through stakeholder exchanges and the Agency's ongoing practical work on AI development.

https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/HotTo.brief: The IMO introduced a new International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS Code) in May 2026, which became effective on 1 July 2026. A ship is considered a MASS only when autonomous or remote technologies replace or support crew functions and it holds a valid MASS Safety Certificate; enhanced automation alone does not qualify. The Code offers voluntary, technology-neutral guidance that complements existing regulations and defines operating conditions, limits, and responses when those limits are exceeded, creating a “goal-based framework” for safe design, operation, and certification. Trials under interim MSC 110 guidelines in June 2019 have shown that larger remotely controlled and autonomous ships are feasible, and while no SOLAS cargo ships are yet operating autonomously, the IMO anticipates commercial service in the near future with a gradual evolution toward more advanced MASS. An IMO seminar in April 2024 addressed the implications, challenges, and opportunities of MASS for ports and public authorities.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open robotics models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model's licence, download count and release date, and is refreshed daily. It states that the data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page was last verified on 2026-10-04 and gives citation details for referencing it. It also notes that searches cover the full text of every published page on the site, all built from the same database.
